```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(comment = NA)
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(tidyverse)
  library(fixest)
  library(modelsummary)
})
```

## A home's price reflects its characteristics

- A hedonic model explains price with the home's characteristics: size, age, bathrooms, location, and time of sale.
- Regression estimates how price varies with each characteristic, **holding the others fixed**.

::: {.key-point}
"Holding the others fixed" is what a regression adds to a scatter plot.
:::

## Two packages

```{r}
#| eval: false
install.packages(c("fixest", "modelsummary"))  # once, in the Console
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(fixest)        # estimate regressions
library(modelsummary)  # build regression tables
```

## Sample: Vancouver strata sales, 2016–2025

```{r}
#| label: sample
bca <- read_rds("data/bca262.rds")

condo <- bca |>
  filter(juris_label == "City of Vancouver", act_use_cat == "Strata Res") |>
  mutate(sale_year = year(sale_date),
         age = sale_year - year_built,
         type = if_else(act_use_name == "Row Housing (Single Unit Ownership)",
                        "Townhouse", "Condo")) |>
  filter(between(sale_year, 2016, 2025))

nrow(condo)
```

## Look at the outcome before you model it

```{r}
#| label: price-hist
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.2
ggplot(condo, aes(price)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 60) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  labs(x = "Sale price (log scale)", y = "Sales")
```

A few sales near `r scales::label_dollar(scale = 1e-6, suffix = " million", accuracy = 1)(max(condo$price))` stretch the axis. What are they, and are all sales market sales?

## Check the extremes

```{r}
#| label: extremes
condo |>
  slice_max(price, n = 4) |>
  select(sale_date, price, floorarea, neigh_label)
```

The top sales are penthouses and large units: unusual, but plausible market sales.

## Look for bulk sales

```{r}
#| label: bulk-count
condo |> count(sale_date, price, sort = TRUE) |> head(3)
```

```{r}
#| label: bulk
#| include: false
bulk <- condo |> count(sale_date, price, sort = TRUE) |> slice(1)
bulk_rows <- semi_join(condo, bulk, by = c("sale_date", "price"))
```

::: {.warning}
`r bulk$n` units sold on one day at an identical `r scales::label_dollar()(bulk$price)`: one building sold as a block, with the price split evenly. Decide how to handle rows like these before you model, and say what you did.
:::

::: {.notes}
- The `r bulk$n` units are all at `r bulk_rows$str_no[1]` `r str_to_title(bulk_rows$str_name[1])` St. `r sum(is.na(bulk_rows$floorarea))` of them have no floor area, so the regressions below drop them anyway.
- Prices are right-skewed, which is why we model log(price).
:::

## Reading coefficients in a log model

| Model | A coefficient of *b* means |
|---|---|
| `log(price) ~ x` | One more unit of *x* is linked to about 100 × *b* % higher price. |
| `log(price) ~ log(x)` | 1% more *x* is linked to about *b* % higher price. |

::: {.key-point}
The second form is an elasticity. We use it for floor area.
:::

## Start with one variable

```{r}
#| label: m1
#| message: true
m1 <- feols(log(price) ~ log(floorarea), data = condo)
m1
```

## fixest drops rows it cannot use

Read the note at the top of the output.

```{r}
#| label: nobs
nobs(m1)
nrow(condo)
```

::: {.warning}
The model dropped `r nrow(condo) - nobs(m1)` sales, the ones with no floor area, including the `r bulk$n` bulk-sale units. Ask whether the missing rows differ from the rest.
:::

## Add more characteristics

```{r}
#| label: m2
m2 <- feols(log(price) ~ log(floorarea) + bedrooms + full_bath + age + type,
            data = condo)
coeftable(m2) |> round(4)
```

## The reference level sets the meaning of a dummy

- `type` has two levels. R uses the first, "Condo", as the reference.
- `typeTownhouse` compares townhouses with condos of the same size, bedrooms, bathrooms, and age.

```{r}
#| label: relevel
condo_th <- condo |> mutate(type = fct_relevel(type, "Townhouse"))
feols(log(price) ~ log(floorarea) + bedrooms + full_bath + age + type,
      data = condo_th) |> coef() |> round(4)
```

The sign flips: now the coefficient compares condos with townhouses.

## Fixed effects compare like with like

```{r}
#| label: m3
m3 <- feols(log(price) ~ log(floorarea) + bedrooms + full_bath + age + type |
              neigh_label + sale_year, data = condo)
coeftable(m3) |> round(4)
```

`| neigh_label + sale_year` compares sales in the same neighbourhood and the same year. It is the same as adding a dummy for every neighbourhood and every year.

## Compare models side by side

```{r}
#| label: msummary-code
#| eval: false
modelsummary(
  list("Size only" = m1, "Characteristics" = m2, "Fixed effects" = m3),
  stars = TRUE,
  gof_map = c("nobs", "r.squared"),
  coef_omit = "Intercept"
)
```

- Each model is a column; standard errors are in parentheses.
- `gof_map` picks the summary rows; `coef_omit` hides the intercept.

## Three models of condo prices

::: {.small}
```{r}
#| label: msummary
#| echo: false
modelsummary(
  list("Size only" = m1, "Characteristics" = m2, "Fixed effects" = m3),
  stars = TRUE,
  gof_map = c("nobs", "r.squared"),
  coef_omit = "Intercept"
)
```
:::

## Why did the bedroom coefficient change?

- Without fixed effects: for the same floor area, more bedrooms means smaller rooms, and multi-bedroom units are more common in cheaper neighbourhoods.
- With fixed effects, the comparison is within a neighbourhood and year, and the bedroom coefficient shrinks towards zero.

::: {.key-point}
A coefficient depends on what else is in the model.
:::

## Choose standard errors on purpose

- `fixest` reports IID standard errors by default.
- Sales in the same neighbourhood share shocks we do not observe, so cluster by neighbourhood.

```{r}
#| label: cluster
summary(m3, vcov = ~neigh_label) |> coeftable() |> round(4)
```

::: {.notes}
Compare with the previous slide: with clustered standard errors, only floor area and age remain clearly different from zero. The townhouse and bathroom coefficients were "significant" only under IID errors.
:::

## Coefficients are associations, not causal effects

- Older buildings sell for less, but they also differ in layout, amenities, and maintenance.
- To claim that *X* changes prices, you need a research design, such as a policy change that affects some homes and not others.

::: {.warning}
This is why the group project avoids simple "distance to X vs. price" correlations.
:::

## Practice

For **single-family** sales (`act_use_cat == "S/F Res"`) in the City of Vancouver, 2016–2025:

1. Regress `log(price)` on `log(floorarea)`, `log(lotsize)`, and `age`, with neighbourhood and sale-year fixed effects.
2. Cluster the standard errors by neighbourhood.
3. How many sales does the model drop, and why?
4. Compare the floor-area elasticity with the one for condos.

## Answer

```{r include=params$answers}
#| label: practice-answer
sfd <- bca |>
  filter(juris_label == "City of Vancouver", act_use_cat == "S/F Res") |>
  mutate(sale_year = year(sale_date), age = sale_year - year_built) |>
  filter(between(sale_year, 2016, 2025))

m_sfd <- feols(log(price) ~ log(floorarea) + log(lotsize) + age |
                 neigh_label + sale_year, data = sfd, vcov = ~neigh_label)
```

## Answer: results

::: {.small}
```{r include=params$answers}
#| label: practice-answer-2
coeftable(m_sfd) |> round(4)
nrow(sfd) - nobs(m_sfd)
```

```{r include=params$answers}
#| label: practice-answer-text
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
cat("The model drops ", scales::comma(nrow(sfd) - nobs(m_sfd)), " of ",
    scales::comma(nrow(sfd)), " sales: ", scales::comma(sum(is.na(sfd$lotsize))),
    " have no lot size and ", scales::comma(sum(is.na(sfd$floorarea))),
    " no floor area. For a house, land carries much of the value, so the ",
    "floor-area elasticity is much lower than for condos.", sep = "")
```
:::
